 Fatherhood changes the brain. And it seems to change hiring decisions, too—if a 
 
https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjUwMDZ9AAcAAAAABtpy0Z0u7ODpNl9Mnpf6q0vN5CSWqO8VM0fic_6ZbLDeP_0SkOs6eXg8z_FjYadUy_pBC1WQ8Yd_pGL4ydcjHPee9TALrBAycOyY-bY 
new dad’s first-born is a girl . 
 A study tracked every worker in Denmark over 25 years, and found that when a male boss had a daughter, the ratio of women’s earnings to men’s immediately rose at his firm, as did the share of women it employed. There were too few female managers to test whether motherhood has the same impact.

79491.subject: Data & Insights: Zcash Stays Private; Bitcoin Searches Still Low
79491.body:
The Data and Insights newsletter brings the highlights of the week from The Block’s Data Dashboard

( https://www.theblock.co/data/crypto-markets/spot )

Presented by:

BRON ( https://bron.org/?utm_source=TheBlock&utm_medium=Email&utm_campaign=DailyNewsletter )

GM, data bulls! Hope you’re enjoying BTC at $85k! With Q4 around the corner, we’re watching markets continue to develop as people get comfortable with crypto again. Our team recently set up a new newsletter titled "Tokenization Briefing." With trillions of dollars of real-world assets migrating onto blockchain rails, we are introducing a way for readers to keep up to date with market insights and visual analyses on what matters in the world of Tokenization. Sign up here ( https://www.theblock.co/newsletters ).

This week, we’re taking a look at ZEC’s privacy developments and crypto web traffic volume. We’ll also look at ETF volumes, perpetuals on prediction markets, and Robinhood chain again. So grab a drink, take a seat, and let's dive in.

1: Staying Private

( https://www.theblock.co/data/on-chain-metrics/comparison-bitcoin-ethereum-solana/zcash-shielded-supply )

Chart via The Block's Data Dashboard

*Key Insights* provided by The Block Research

* Nearly 5 million ZEC sit in shielded pools, roughly 23% of the supply. This matches nearly the 5.15 million peak from late May, before a headline about vulnerabilities in the Orchard pool caused 750k ZEC to withdraw.

* Since then, ZEC users have migrated to Ironwood, a new pool with mechanisms to verify that the full balance is backed.

* As a reminder, Zcash privacy is opt-in. The majority of tokens live in transparent addresses that act like Bitcoin; senders, recipients, and amounts are all visible. Only when coins are shielded by moving into one of the zero-knowledge pools do the coins become private.

* Sprout, Sapling, and Orchard are all previous pools that still hold residual balance, but the vast majority of supply going forward will be held in the Ironwood pool.

* Orchard held a peak of 4.5 million ZEC tokens shortly before the vulnerability was discussed publicly. Ironwood already holds 3.9 million tokens despite only launching in July. Growth for this pool continues, now taking up 80% of the shielded supply market share.

* Despite setbacks with Orchard, privacy remains a growth vector for Zcash as users increasingly explore the privacy features ZEC offers. Ironwood likely continues to be the go-to pool while more of the supply is shielded and private.

79487.subject: 🧥 Huang says the doomers are bluffing
79487.body:
The Atlas

Автор: GenAI Works


Автор: GenAI Works

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/huang-says-doomers-bluffing-genai-works-2hqxf?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3B9YvPwo9SR4Gx8J862A0g0Q%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=0Tw-RIFOuMecs1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~mubdb5io~wc-null-null&eid=fz96fz-mubdb5io-wc
  
Welcome back! Jensen Huang accused the safety crowd of asking for the opposite of what they claim, Anthropic built a lab where Claude runs the robots, and OpenAI published six things its models got caught doing.  In today's Atlas Newsletter: Huang says the safety crowd is asking for something else: What does he think they're really after? Anthropic puts more into biology: What costs $10,000 that Claude just did for $150? OpenAI published six things its models did wrong: What was the model hiding in its notes to itself? Cloudflare's vulnerability harness started as one skill: Why does the verifier's job start with trying to disprove the finding? PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions. Huang says the safety crowd is asking for something else Jensen Huang went on CBS on Sunday and accused frontier lab leaders of arguing in bad faith. His line: "Go and read between the lines. They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have." Then: "They must be doing it for ulterior reasons." Asked what those reasons are, he said he didn't know, and called scaring people about the technology irresponsible and unnecessary. Worth checking his claim against the essay he's responding to.  Amodei's "We Must Pace the Frontier" proposes three things, and one of them asks the US government to regulate frontier labs specifically, on antitrust grounds.  Regulation aimed at the handful of companies at the top is a different request from regulation of the industry, which is roughly Huang's point. Altman amplified the essay. So did Musk. Huang's own position has not moved. A slowdown among US labs cedes ground to China, the labs can slow themselves down without asking Washington, and the rules already on the books just need enforcing. He now has company.  Trump posted Saturday that his administration will not hinder the growth of the industry. Michael Kratsios, who runs the White House science and technology office, told Fox on Sunday that labs worried about their products could simply stop. Two weeks ago Huang told a Goldman Sachs conference that alarm about AI security is good for the security business, asking what better way there is to create demand than to create a problem. He also sells the chips every side of this argument runs on. Master

When Intelligence Gets Cheap, Where Does the Value Go? For the last few years, AI has been dominated by one question: Who has the best model? GPT vs Claude vs Gemini vs Qwen vs DeepSeek. Better reasoning. Bigger context windows. Lower prices. Better benchmarks. But I think we're approaching a much more interesting question: What happens when many models become good enough? Because when intelligence gets cheaper and more abundant, the value doesn't disappear. It moves. See their unique perspectives on how to shape agentic AI strategy, from architectural patterns and evaluation to comprehensive security and deployment. Learn how to: Build, monitor, and govern responsible AI agents at scale. Enhance agent performance and decision-making. Find the right AI architecture for your business needs. 👉 Get your digital copy 1. The model can be differentiated without being the moat Think about Coke and Pepsi. They aren't identical. The sweetness is different. The carbonation is different. The taste is different. But those differences don't fully explain why these companies became enormous. The real moat extends far beyond the formula: Brand. Distribution. Availability. Portfolio. Customer relationships. Habit. Trust. I think foundation models could follow a similar path. One model might be slightly better at coding. Another at reasoning. Another might be cheaper or faster. But if five models can successfully complete the same task, a small benchmark advantage may matter less than: Context → Data → Workflow → Distribution → Trust The model still matters. It just may not be where the entire moat lives. 2. When abundance arrives, scarcity moves There is a useful economic pattern here: When something valuable becomes abundant, value tends to move toward whatever remains scarce. We've seen this before. The internet made information abundant. Attention became scarce. GPS made location intelligence abundant. That helped unlock ride sharing, delivery, logistics and location-based services.
